summary: The top hypothesis (confidence 0.55, medium) is that config change cfg-3120 on pricing-engine — ramping flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 12:04Z — moved all quote computation onto the CPU-expensive GreeksV2 calculator path, saturating pricing-engine CPU (~40%→99%) and pushing p99 from ~60ms to ~2.6s, which blew order-service's 2000ms quote budget. This is clearly ahead of the field (next: organic capacity saturation at 0.30) and is supported by co-timed CPU/latency onset, an error signature explicitly naming calculator=GreeksV2, and the market-data-service deploy (dep-6111) showing zero errors. Confidence is capped at medium because the metric bucket size (420s) prevents ordering cfg-3120's 12:04 timestamp against the true onset within the 11:58→12:05 interval, so a purely organic volume-driven saturation cannot be fully excluded. We recommend an immediate rollback of cfg-3120 to 5% (or pausing the GreeksV2 ramp) as a safe, reversible mitigation, with request_rate/depth checks run in parallel to discriminate H1 from H2.

ranked_hypotheses.title: cfg-3120 GreeksV2 100% ramp saturated pricing-engine CPU
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Config change cfg-3120 on pricing-engine ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 12:04Z, switching all quote computation to the GreeksV2 calculator path. GreeksV2 is materially more CPU-expensive than the prior default, so pricing-engine CPU went from ~40% to ~99% and per-request compute latency rose to ~2.6s, blowing the 2000ms quote budget. order-service, which calls pricing-engine synchronously for quotes, then timed out.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 on pricing-engine at 12:04Z, routing all quote traffic to the GreeksV2 calculator
GreeksV2 computation is more expensive, driving pricing-engine CPU from ~40% to 99-100% saturated
CPU saturation raises per-request quote compute time, p99 60ms -> ~2600ms, exceeding the 2000ms budget
order-service's synchronous pricing-engine quote call then exceeds its 2500ms client timeout

assumptions: GreeksV2 is more CPU-expensive than the preceding default path (not directly measured)
request_rate/depth did not also rise sharply at the same time (not checked)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Organic capacity saturation (market-open quote volume) on pricing-engine, HIST-113-like
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A surge in quote request volume/recursion depth exceeded provisioned pricing-engine capacity (CPU), pinning it at 99-100% and pushing p99 to ~2.6s. The GreeksV2 ramp is a coincidental bystander; the true trigger is load outgrowing provisioned capacity, exactly matching historical incident HIST-113 (same symptom pair, capacity_saturation, fixed by raising replicas).

causal_chain.claim: Quote request volume/load rises beyond provisioned pricing-engine capacity
p99 latency rises ~43x to ~2600ms, exceeding budget and client timeout

assumptions: A load/volume increase occurred in the 11:58-12:05 window (request_rate not queried)
cfg-3120's 12:04 timing is coincidental rather than causal

ranked_hypotheses.title: dep-6111 protobuf serialization change broke pricing-engine's parsing of market-data-service quotes
ranked_hypotheses.statement: market-data-service v5.2.0 switched quote serialization to protobuf at 11:56Z. pricing-engine, which calls market-data-service on the quote path, cannot correctly parse the new payload, causing retries/wasteful fallback compute that saturates CPU and blows the compute deadline. The reporter's stated suspicion.

causal_chain.claim: dep-6111 switches market-data-service quote payloads to protobuf at 11:56Z
pricing-engine (the caller) cannot parse/handle the new format, retrying or falling back and burning CPU
pricing-engine CPU saturates and quote compute exceeds deadline

assumptions: pricing-engine parses market-data-service payloads in a way incompatible with protobuf
the (de)serialization breakage manifests only as CPU-bound retries rather than parse errors

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation (cold cache / failover) on the quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache, shared by pricing-engine and market-data-service, degraded (cold cache or failover), forcing pricing-engine to recompute quotes from source and saturating CPU. Matches HIST-107 cold-cache storm precedent.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache cold/failed, cache misses on the quote path
pricing-engine recomputes from source, driving CPU to 99%
quote latency blows budget -> order-service timeout

assumptions: redis-cache actually degraded (no redis metrics were queried)

facts.statement: The first order-service quote timeout occurred at 12:06:10Z, with the message 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms'; all 225 error logs in the window share a single timeout pattern (no serialization errors).
pricing-engine latency_p99_ms was stable at ~59-60ms through 11:58, then jumped to ~2600ms (max 2849ms) in the 12:05 bucket and stayed there.
pricing-engine cpu_pct was ~40% through 11:58, then saturated to ~99% (max 100%) starting in the same 12:05 bucket and stayed pinned for the rest of the window.
order-service latency_p99_ms rose from ~150ms baseline to ~2400-2970ms in the same 12:05 bucket, tracking the pricing-engine onset.

Exactly one config/flag change existed in the window: cfg-3120 on pricing-engine, key flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100 at 12:04:00Z by pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic').
Only one deployment occurred across all services in 11:30-13:59: dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0 ('Switch quote serialization to protobuf'), deployed 11:56:00Z, status live, rolled_back_at null.

market-data-service logged zero errors between 08:00Z and 13:59Z; its only log in that span was a benign TLS WARN at 11:43:53Z — no error or latency symptom despite the report blaming its serialization change.
order-service's quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service; order-service does not call market-data-service directly.
cfg-3120's timestamp (12:04:00Z) sits between the 11:58-12:05 latency/CPU onset bucket and is ~2 minutes before the first order-service quote timeout at 12:06:10Z.

Historical precedents match the 'quote timeouts' + 'cpu 99%' pattern (HIST-113 capacity saturation; HIST-107 redis cold-cache storm; HIST-101 bad deployment); these are leads, not evidence about this incident.
A complete retried get_config_changes returned exactly one config change (cfg-3120), following an initial partial result due to a config-audit shard being down.

assumptions: ASSUMPTION: GreeksV2 is materially more CPU-expensive than the preceding default calculator path (statically inferred, not directly measured).
ASSUMPTION: request_rate / recursion depth did not also rise sharply at the same time (not checked), which is required to separate H1 from H2.
ASSUMPTION: cfg-3120 took effect promptly at 12:04:00Z rather than being batched/delayed.
ASSUMPTION: The absence of serialization errors established for ERROR-level streams of the three named services generalizes sufficiently to weaken H3.
ASSUMPTION: The retried complete get_config_changes (count 1) accurately enumerates the window's config changes despite the initial shard outage.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately roll back cfg-3120: revert flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 100 back to 5 (or 0) on pricing-engine to take traffic off the GreeksV2 calculator path.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change aligned with the 11:58->12:05 CPU/latency onset and the 12:06:10 product failure; reverting is reversible, low-risk, and directly tests H1 by restoring the prior calculator path.

recommended_actions.action: In parallel, query pricing-engine request_rate / recursion depth / quote volume for 11:50-12:10 at the finest available resolution to test whether load rose independently of cfg-3120.
recommended_actions.rationale: Discriminates H1 (flag-driven CPU) from H2 (organic capacity saturation); without this the two remain indistinguishable on CPU metrics alone.

recommended_actions.action: After rollback, confirm recovery: verify pricing-engine cpu_pct returns toward ~40% and p99 returns to ~60ms, and that order-service quote timeouts cease.
recommended_actions.rationale: Validates that cfg-3120 was the cause; failure to recover would point to H2 (capacity) or a shared-component cause (H4).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back dep-6111 (market-data-service v5.2.0) as a first action; if it remains suspect, first check pricing-engine for parse/(de)serialization errors on the market-data-service call path before acting.
recommended_actions.rationale: market-data-service shows zero errors (F3) and is only transitively on order-service's path (F10/F15), so it is a weak candidate; an unwarranted rollback could destabilize other callers.

recommended_actions.action: Query redis-cache (and ledger-db/kafka) cache-hit/miss, latency, and availability metrics for the window to confirm/deny a shared-datastore contribution.
recommended_actions.rationale: Closes the shared-component hypothesis (H4, HIST-107 precedent); a cache-miss storm would show miss/latency symptoms, not calculator CPU saturation.

recommended_actions.action: If load (not the flag) is the driver, raise pricing-engine replica count / CPU allocation as the mitigation, mirroring the HIST-113 resolution.
recommended_actions.rationale: Provides the alternative remedy if request_rate confirms organic capacity saturation (H2).

recommended_actions.action: Adopt guarded rollout for CPU-heavy calculator experiment flags: require canary/staged ramp with CPU and p99 SLO gates and automatic rollback instead of a 5->100 jump.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents recurrence of an instant all-traffic ramp onto a CPU-expensive path (the cfg-3120 5->100 change).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument pricing-engine per-calculator CPU cost/latency and alarm on calculator-path CPU saturation and quote p99 breaching budget, with correlation to in-flight config changes.
recommended_actions.rationale: Would have caught the GreeksV2 CPU cost directly and made CPU/flag correlation explicit, addressing the measurement gap behind the H1/H2 ambiguity.

data_gaps: pricing-engine memory_pct, error_rate, request_rate, restarts, and thread/pool metrics were not queried; memory/pool/thread exhaustion or restarts on the quote path cannot be ruled out.
Metric bucketing at 420s prevents resolving the true onset below the 11:58->12:05 interval, so cfg-3120 (12:04) cannot be definitively ordered against onset — the key limitation for H1 vs H2.

No metric queries were run for pricing-engine, market-data-service, redis-cache, ledger-db, or kafka dependencies, so no dependency-level metric evidence exists to confirm/deny a shared-component cause.
Serialization-error absence is established only for ERROR-level streams of the three named services; a broad multi-service/multi-level scan was not performed.
The initial get_config_changes was partial (config-audit shard 2/3 down); enumeration relies on the retry, leaving residual risk of an unseen config change.
No deployment diff/compatibility data for the dep-6111 protobuf switch, so whether it broke internal callers (e.g. pricing-engine parsing) is unconfirmed.
No historical precedent with a serialization/payload-incompatibility root cause was found, so H3 has no confirming precedent either way.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that quote request_rate/recursion depth rose sharply at ~12:04-12:05 independent of cfg-3120, which would favor organic capacity saturation (H2) and demote the config change to a coincidental bystander.
Demonstration that reverting cfg-3120 does NOT restore CPU/p99/latency, which would falsify H1.
Pricing-engine logs/metrics showing parse or (de)serialization errors on the market-data-service call path, which would revive H3.
redis-cache (or ledger-db/kafka) metrics showing a cold-cache/failover storm coincident with onset, which would support H4.
Pricing-engine memory/thread/pool saturation or restarts coincident with onset, indicating a cause other than the GreeksV2 computation path.
Finer-resolution metrics showing CPU/latency onset clearly BEFORE 12:04 (i.e. before cfg-3120), which would undercut H1's causal timing.

findings.statement: Dependency graph confirms order-service's quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http), with pricing-engine also depending on redis-cache (cache) and market-data-service also depending on redis-cache. So market-data-service is only reachable from order-service transitively through pricing-engine.

redis-cache is a shared:true datastore with multiple upstream consumers (auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service), so it is a plausible shared-component path; however T1 reported no serialization/deserialization errors and the pricing-engine failure mode is CPU saturation (99-100%) on GreeksV2 computation, which a cache miss storm would not by itself explain. A cold-cache storm (HIST-107) would be expected to show cache-miss symptoms, not 100% CPU pinned on the calculator.

Historical precedents for the exact symptom pair ('quote timeouts' + 'cpu 99%' on pricing-engine) exist: HIST-113 (2026-01-28) root cause 'Record market-open volume exceeded provisioned capacity' (capacity_saturation, resolution raised replica count). HIST-107 (2025-12-09) is a shared-redis cold-cache storm with 'quote latency'. HIST-101 (2025-08-14) is a bad_deployment whose symptom included 'high cpu'. These are leads only, not evidence about this incident.

findings.statement: RANKED CANDIDATE ASSESSMENT — (1) cfg-3120 GreeksV2 100% ramp at 12:04 is the leading candidate: it is the only change whose timing aligns with the 11:58->12:05 CPU/latency onset and the 12:06:10 product-visible failure, its owner service is the degraded dependency, and the error names calculator=GreeksV2. Supporting: pricing-engine CPU 40%->99% and p99 60ms->2600ms in the same bucket. (2) dep-6111 protobuf deploy at 11:56 is a weaker candidate: it predates onset by ~8 min and market-data-service shows zero errors (F3), contradicting a serialization defect there; the serialization change would also be expected to produce (de)serialization errors, which T1 found none of. (3) shared redis-cache is a lower-ranked shared-component hypothesis, unsupported so far because no cache-miss/latency signal from market-data-service or auth/portfolio was reported. (4) pure capacity saturation (HIST-113-like) cannot be excluded and would be indistinguishable from the flag ramp on CPU metrics alone.
